title: Old Obsessions with New Justifications — Eddie Would Go
units: Opinion · 8 min read
Old Obsessions with New Justifications
The ghosts of twentieth-century geopolitics return with force to contemporary debate, this time with renewed arguments.
12 March 2026 · Opinion
«The strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must»
— Thucydides, The Peloponnesian War

When a president-elect in the United States takes office, the design of the Oval Office and the arrangement of presidential portraits, busts and sculptures send a deliberate political message. Joe Biden placed a portrait of Franklin D. Roosevelt in preparation for his new industrial policy; Donald Trump, in his first term, opted for Andrew Jackson, who was called — and considered himself — the first popular, or populist, president. In his second term, a figure regaining prominence is William McKinley.

McKinley is not among the best-known presidents, partly because he was assassinated during his first term and succeeded by the overwhelming figure of Teddy Roosevelt (to the point that the school in the series Glee bears his name as a nod to this historical neglect). Why does Trump put the focus on him? McKinley was the architect of a policy of steep protective tariffs and the president who expanded US territory after the war with Spain. In this context, the gaze towards Greenland takes on new meaning. It is no recent whim: Washington's relationship with the island has oscillated for a century and a half between geopolitical fascination and strategic calculation — whoever controls this piece will dominate the Arctic.

The obsession is not new. It dates back to 1867, when Secretary of State William H. Seward, after the purchase of Alaska, set his sights on the Danish possession. For him, Greenland was the logical next piece: a future source of coal for the fleet, a whaling bastion and a counterweight to British influence from Canada. His approaches to Denmark (1867-68) failed against a sceptical Congress, but the idea was planted.

The spark was urgently rekindled in 1941. After the Nazi occupation of Denmark, the US invoked a Monroe Doctrine for the Arctic, unilaterally assuming the "protection" of Greenland. This established a permanent military presence, formalised in the Defence Treaty of 1951. Washington obtained rights to establish bases.

During the climax of the Cold War, Greenland became a strategic region for American military deployment. The cornerstone was Thule Air Base, established in 1951. It was not the only one. The Ballistic Missile Early Warning System (BMEWS) was deployed there in the early 1960s, with massive radars to detect a Soviet attack across the North Pole. In addition, a network of early warning stations (the DEW Line and later projects) and seismic and submarine monitoring sites dotted the coast. At its peak, Thule housed more than 10,000 American military and civilian personnel, making it one of the largest and most strategic bases outside the continental territory. The presence was so vast that Denmark, though an ally, maintained frequent diplomatic tensions over sovereignty on the territory where the bases operated.

It was in this context that the Truman administration made a formal offer to Denmark in 1946: 100 million dollars in exchange for full sovereignty over Greenland. The rejection was categorical, and from the end of the Cold War until today interest in Greenland steadily declined, as did the number of troops deployed there.
The Revival of Interest: Minerals, China and Melting Ice

The interest mutated, but it did not fade. In 2019, Donald Trump's confirmation of his wish to buy the island provoked a diplomatic crisis. Far from a mere whim, it was the expression of a renewed strategic anxiety. The new objective was to contain China, which under the label of a "near-Arctic State" had identified the twin value of the melting ice: resources and routes.

Greenland is a storehouse of critical minerals. Its deposits contain some of the largest reserves of rare earth elements (REE) outside China, elements essential for permanent magnets in wind turbines, electric vehicles and precision weapons systems.

Kvanefjeld (Kuannersuit) Project This deposit in the south, one of the most controversial, holds resources estimated at more than 1 billion tonnes of ore, containing rare earths (REE oxides) and uranium. A report by the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland (GEUS) indicates that it contains one of the largest REE reserves in the world.
Kringlerne Project Another significant rare earth deposit, with estimates exceeding 600 million tonnes of mineral resource.
Other Critical Elements Besides REE, Greenland has important prospects of graphite, cobalt, nickel, zirconium and heavy rare earths, all vital to the energy transition and to high technology.

Chinese participation in Kvanefjeld through Shenghe Resources set off alarms in Washington. The subsequent decision by the Greenlandic autonomous government (2021) to ban uranium mining — and de facto freeze the project — was a strategic relief for the West, but it laid bare the battle over resources.
Arctic shipping routes and Greenland

Global warming is acting as a geo-economic catalyst in the far north, transforming the Arctic from an impassable ice barrier into a vital artery for world trade. The retreat of the ice would open three main corridors: the Northern Sea Route (NSR) along the Russian coast, the Northwest Passage (NWP), which crosses the Canadian archipelago and skirts Greenland, and the future Transpolar Sea Route (TSR), which would cross the centre of the ocean. These routes are not merely geographical alternatives; they represent a reduction of up to 40% in sailing time between the ports of northeast Asia and northern Europe. In practical terms this means cutting roughly 15 days of transit compared with the traditional Suez Canal route, which translates into massive fuel savings, lower operating costs and a drastic reduction in the carbon footprint of global logistics.

For Greenland, this thaw redefines its sovereign value, positioning it as the "Gibraltar of the North". Sitting at the confluence of these routes, the island ceases to be a remote territory and becomes the sentinel guarding access to the North Atlantic. This new centrality has unleashed competition among the great powers: while Russia claims sovereignty over much of the Northern Sea Route and China promotes its concept of the "Polar Silk Road", the United States seeks to consolidate Greenland as a strategic partner capable of offering deep-water ports and logistical services that guarantee freedom of navigation. Control of these jurisdictional waters is no longer merely a question of territorial defence but of dominance over the future node of intercontinental trade.

This opening, however, poses a paradox of security and environment. The increase in maritime traffic in previously pristine waters demands a search, rescue and environmental disaster response infrastructure that is currently limited. For Washington, ensuring that Nuuk (the Greenlandic capital) has the Western technology and investment to manage these routes is a priority. As analysts at Harvard's Belfer Center have warned, mastery of Arctic logistics will be as decisive for twenty-first century hegemony as control of the seas was for the powers of the nineteenth, turning the thaw into a race against time for influence over the new map of world power.
The Greenlandic Will: Polls and Self-Determination

Greenlandic domestic politics is a decisive factor. Recent surveys, such as those conducted by the Institute of Social Studies at the University of Greenland (Ilisimatusarfik), show a population deeply divided between economic development based on large-scale mining and the protection of the environment and traditional culture. A referendum in 2008 approved an expanded self-government statute with 75% support, a key step towards independence. A referendum in 2021 in the municipality of Sermersooq (which includes Nuuk) on uranium and rare earth mining reflected the local division, preceding the national decision to ban it. The narrative of independence is powerful, but it collides with economic dependence on the annual Danish subsidy (approximately 600 million dollars), which represents more than a third of the Greenlandic budget. The island's inhabitants waver between independence and continued autonomy within the Kingdom of Denmark. Three days ago, all political parties rejected the idea of becoming part of the United States.
Conclusion

The central problem no longer lies in demonstrating Greenland's strategic importance but in understanding the real effectiveness of the strategy articulated from Washington. The purchase proposal under the Trump administration, though symptomatic of a historic geopolitical anxiety, can be read as a strategic anachronism that diverted attention from more solid and readily available tools.
A Critique of the Transactional View

The 1951 Defence Treaty remains in force and, within the NATO framework — now reinforced by the accession of Sweden and its Arctic capability — the deployment of troops and surveillance systems to counter Russian and Chinese activity in the region is legitimate and operationally superior to any annexation adventure. The purchase suggestion exposed a contradiction: while transatlantic ties with key allies such as Denmark were being weakened through rhetoric, the aim was to acquire a territory whose defence was already guaranteed by that same alliance. The most effective strategy for reducing Russian influence in the Arctic runs not through unilateral gestures but through strengthening NATO's cohesion and resolving its internal conflicts, presenting a unified front.

As for access to critical minerals, the principal obstacle is neither Danish sovereignty nor a hypothetical exclusion of the United States. The concessions are available, but they are shot through with the local population's determination to protect its environment and its way of life. The 2021 decision to ban uranium mining and freeze the Kvanefjeld project is a clear message that Nuuk will not be a simple supplier of resources. Here, competition with China is won not with money or blunt diplomatic pressure but with the capacity to offer sustainable mining technology, local training and agreements that prioritise Greenland's long-term development — something the Chinese extractive model does not necessarily promise.

The reactivation of American Arctic diplomacy — modernising Thule Base and deploying EXIM credits — is a step in the right direction, but insufficient if a purely military and economic logic of "containment" is maintained. The persistent obsession with Greenland, from Seward to Trump, reveals a constant: the search for security through control. The current challenge, however, is to invert that equation.

Real power in the twenty-first century Arctic will be measured not solely by who controls bases but by who wins legitimacy, trust and durable alliances. The next phase will be written not with purchase offers but with the capacity of Washington and its allies to offer Greenland an attractive and respectful partnership for its sovereign development. Hegemony in the Arctic is no longer bought; it is negotiated and won with a value proposition that Greenland, at last, can choose for itself. Otherwise, the obsession with controlling the island could end up isolating the United States in the very region it most yearns to dominate — and from one of its most important alliances. We shall see whether the worst scenes of the Peloponnesian War return to our own era.
